description: Sensation vs perception, and the monocular and binocular cues we use to judge distance.
content_html:
Sensation and Perception

When light enters your eye, your retina detects it. But detecting the light is not the same as understanding what you are looking at. Psychologists draw a crucial distinction between sensation and perception. Sensation is the physical detection of stimuli by the sense organs — it is passive and automatic. Perception is the brain’s active interpretation of those signals to create a meaningful experience of the world.

A simple example illustrates the difference: your eye detects a patch of reflected light (sensation), but your brain interprets it as a red apple sitting on a table (perception). The same raw data reaches the retina, but perception gives it meaning. This distinction matters because it opens the question of what shapes perception — is it driven mainly by the raw information available (as Gibson argued) or mainly by our prior knowledge and experience (as Gregory argued)?

Key Fact

Sensation is the passive detection of physical energy by sense organs. Perception is the brain’s active interpretation of that information to create a meaningful experience. All perception begins with sensation, but sensation alone is not perception.

Visual Cues and Depth Perception

One of the brain’s most impressive feats is judging distance and depth from the flat, two-dimensional images formed on the retina. It does this using depth cues. Some cues require only one eye (monocular depth cues); others require both eyes working together (binocular depth cues).

Monocular Depth Cues

Monocular depth cues can be detected with just one eye. There are four you need to know:

Height in plane — objects that appear higher in the visual field (closer to the horizon) are perceived as further away. Think of a field of people: those near the horizon appear in the upper part of your visual field and are seen as more distant.

Relative size — when two objects are known to be the same size, the one that projects a smaller image on the retina is perceived as further away. A friend who appears smaller in your view is interpreted as being further away, not as having physically shrunk.

Occlusion — when one object partially blocks another from view, the partially blocked object is perceived as further away. The blocking object is seen as being in front. This is one of the most reliable monocular cues.

Linear perspective — parallel lines (like railway tracks or a straight road) appear to converge at a distant vanishing point. The closer together the lines appear, the further away that part of the scene is judged to be.

Key Fact

The four monocular depth cues are: height in plane (higher in visual field = further), relative size (smaller image = further), occlusion (blocked object = further), and linear perspective (converging lines = further). These can all be detected with one eye.

Binocular Depth Cues

Binocular depth cues depend on having two eyes. Because our eyes are set a short distance apart, each eye receives a slightly different view of the same scene. The brain uses this difference to calculate depth.

Retinal disparity is the difference between the images received by the left and right eyes. Because the eyes are set apart, nearby objects create a larger difference between the two images than distant objects do. The brain uses the size of this disparity to calculate how far away an object is. Close objects have greater disparity; distant objects have less. You can experience this by holding a finger close to your face and alternately closing each eye — notice how the finger appears to jump sideways.

Convergence is the way both eyes turn inward (converge) to focus on a nearby object. The closer the object, the more the eyes must converge. The brain detects the muscular effort involved in converging and uses this as information about how close the object is. When you focus on something very close — the end of your own nose, for example — you can feel the slight strain of convergence. For objects far away, almost no convergence is needed.

Monocular Versus Binocular Cues: Key Differences

A useful way to remember the distinction between monocular and binocular cues is to consider what each type depends on. Monocular cues are properties of the visual scene itself — they are present in the pattern of light that reaches the retina and work even in a photograph or painting. This is why artists can create a convincing sense of depth on a flat canvas using linear perspective, relative size and occlusion. You do not need two eyes or a three-dimensional scene to use these cues.

Binocular cues, by contrast, depend on having two eyes that are physically separated. They arise from the geometry of the visual system itself rather than from properties of the scene. Retinal disparity is created by the fact that your eyes are roughly 6–7 centimetres apart; the further apart the viewpoints, the greater the potential disparity for close objects. Convergence is a proprioceptive signal — it comes from muscles in the eye, not from the light pattern.

In practice, the brain uses all available depth cues simultaneously and combines them to produce a single, coherent depth estimate. Binocular cues are particularly useful for judging the distance of close objects (within a few metres), where retinal disparity is largest. Monocular cues remain informative at much greater distances, where the eyes are too far apart for retinal disparity to be measurably different between near and far objects.
exam_tip_html: On questions about depth cues, examiners commonly ask you to identify whether a cue is monocular or binocular and to describe it. Make sure you know all four monocular cues by name — stating ‘perspective’ alone is not enough; you need ‘linear perspective’ and its definition. For application questions, read the scenario carefully to identify which cue is being described — does it require one or two eyes? Is it a physical property of the scene or a muscular signal?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sensation is the passive detection of physical stimuli; perception is the brain’s active interpretation that gives those stimuli meaning. All perception starts with sensation but goes further.
  • Monocular depth cues (usable with one eye) include height in plane, relative size, occlusion, and linear perspective.
  • Binocular depth cues require two eyes: retinal disparity (the difference between left and right eye images) and convergence (the muscular effort of turning both eyes inward to focus on close objects).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a binocular depth cue?
A) Linear perspective
B) Retinal disparity
C) Height in plane
D) Occlusion

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise definition stating that perception is the brain’s active process of interpreting and giving meaning to the raw sensory information received from the senses.
Secure: Clear definition capturing the interpretive, meaningful aspect of perception.
Developing: Partial definition — describes seeing or experiencing without capturing the interpretive, brain-based process.
Emerging: Confuses perception with sensation, e.g. ‘when your eyes detect light.’

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'occlusion' as a monocular depth cue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines occlusion as when one object partially blocks another from view; explains that the blocked object is perceived as further away; developed with a clear example (e.g. a lamp post blocking part of a building in the distance).
Secure: Defines occlusion and explains the depth perception consequence.
Developing: Describes blocking but does not explain the depth perception implication.
Emerging: Vague response or confusion with another depth cue.

practice_questions.text: Priya is looking at a railway line stretching into the distance. The tracks appear to get closer together as they recede. Explain which depth cue Priya is using and why it helps her judge distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies linear perspective; explains that parallel lines appear to converge at a vanishing point as distance increases; links clearly to the scenario (the tracks appearing to come together) and explains that the degree of convergence provides depth information.
Secure: Correct identification with clear explanation engaging the scenario.
Developing: Correct identification but explanation is limited or does not clearly reference the scenario.
Emerging: Names a depth cue without explanation or scenario engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the two binocular depth cues.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Retinal disparity defined as the difference between left and right eye images, with explanation that closer objects produce greater disparity and the brain calculates depth from this; convergence defined as the inward turning of both eyes to focus on close objects, with explanation that greater muscular effort signals closer objects; both described with accurate terminology.
Secure: Both cues described accurately; one may lack a fully developed explanation.
Developing: Both named with partial descriptions; one may be inaccurate.
Emerging: Only one cue described or both very vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the role of depth cues in visual perception.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1): Four monocular cues (height in plane, relative size, occlusion, linear perspective) and two binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence); each described with how it provides depth information; distinction between monocular and binocular.
Evaluation (AO3): Strength — depth cues are supported by consistent everyday observations and demonstrate the sophistication of the visual system. Strength — knowledge of depth cues has practical applications in art, film and virtual reality design. Weakness — monocular depth cues work in 2D images as well as real 3D scenes, suggesting the brain uses inference from experience rather than purely bottom-up information (supporting Gregory over Gibson). Weakness — individual differences exist; people with certain conditions (e.g. amblyopia) may not process binocular cues effectively.
Mastering: Accurate description with at least two developed evaluation points.
Secure: Depth cues described and two evaluation points made.
Developing: Some cues described; one evaluation point.
Emerging: Brief or partial description; evaluation absent or undeveloped.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the key difference between sensation and perception?
options: Sensation is learned; perception is innate
Sensation detects raw stimuli; perception interprets them to give meaning
Sensation requires both eyes; perception requires only one
Sensation is slow; perception is fast

knowledge_checks.q: Which monocular depth cue involves objects higher in the visual field being seen as further away?
The depth cue based on the difference between the images received by the left and right eye is called retinal _____.
When one object partially blocks another, we perceive the blocked object as _____ away.
Match each depth cue to its correct description:
right: The muscular effort of turning both eyes inward to focus on a nearby object
The difference between the images seen by the left and right eye
Parallel lines appearing to meet at a distant vanishing point

flashcard_questions.a: The passive detection of physical stimuli by sense organs and conversion into neural signals.
The brain's active interpretation of sensory information to create a meaningful experience.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four monocular depth cues?
flashcard_questions.a: Height in plane, relative size, occlusion, and linear perspective.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'height in plane' mean as a depth cue?
flashcard_questions.a: Objects higher in the visual field (nearer the horizon) are perceived as further away.

flashcard_questions.q: What is relative size as a depth cue?
flashcard_questions.a: When two objects are the same size, the one casting a smaller retinal image is seen as further away.

flashcard_questions.q: What is occlusion as a depth cue?
flashcard_questions.a: When one object partially blocks another, the blocked object is perceived as further away.
Parallel lines appearing to converge at a vanishing point as they recede into the distance.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two binocular depth cues?

flashcard_questions.a: The difference between the images seen by the left and right eye, used to calculate depth.

flashcard_questions.q: What is convergence as a depth cue?
flashcard_questions.a: The muscular effort of turning both eyes inward to focus on a nearby object.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of depth cue requires two eyes to work?
flashcard_questions.a: Binocular depth cues — retinal disparity and convergence.

glossary_terms.definition: The process by which sense organs detect raw physical energy from the environment and convert it into a neural signal.
The process by which the brain interprets and gives meaning to the raw information received from the senses.
Information in the visual scene that the brain uses to judge distance, depth or three-dimensional structure.
A monocular depth cue in which parallel lines appear to converge towards a vanishing point as they recede into the distance.
The small difference between the images seen by the left and right eye; the brain uses this difference to perceive depth and distance.
A binocular depth cue based on the muscular effort required to turn both eyes inward to focus on a nearby object.

hero_image_caption: Railway tracks converging to a vanishing point demonstrate linear perspective depth cues.
